name: GO Classes CS Test Series 2026 | Computer Networks | Topic Wise Test 1

question.text:
Consider a $1 \mathrm{~Mbps}$ satellite channel with $50 \mathrm{~ms}$ round trip propagation delay. We want to send a $1000$ bit frame, and we will not send a second frame until we receive acknowledgment for the first frame.

What fraction of the available bandwidth are we using?

  1. $1 / 40$
  2. $1 / 51$
  3. $1 / 2$
  4. $1 / 5$

An error-control code with minimum Hamming distance of $11$ is capable of

  1. detecting $11$ bits of error.
  2. detecting $5$ bits of error.
  3. correcting $5$ bits of error.
  4. correcting $11$ bits of error.

Let $\text{CRC}$ generator polynomial $\text{G}(x)=1+x$.

Which of the following errors $\text{E}(x)$ will be detected by $\text{G}(x)?$

  1. $\text{E}(x)=x^{12}+x^{11}+x^3+x^2+x+1$
  2. $\text{E}(x)=x^{36}+x^5+1$
  3. $\text{E}(x)=x^{17}+x^5 $
  4. $\text{E}(x)=x^{11}+x^2+1$

Slotted aloha is a variant of the Aloha media-access protocol that divides time into equal-sized $\text{“slots"}$ and only starts transmissions at the beginning of a slot time. In a slotted aloha system, suppose there are $5$ nodes that each transmit with probability of $p$. What is the probability, in a given slot time, that one of the nodes successfully transmits a packet?

  1. $5 p(1-p)^ 4$
  2. $p(1-p)^ 4$
  3. $(1-p)^ 5$
  4. $p^ 5$

Consider the network of learning bridges shown in the following figure. Learning bridges can learn their forwarding table based on the source $\textsf{MAC}$ address of the incoming packets.

Assuming each initially knows nothing, and two transmissions occur in order -

  1. $\text{B}$ sends to $\text{C}$
  2. $\text{D}$ sends to $\text{B}$

Now suppose if $\text{F}$ sends to $\text{D},$ then which of the following nodes will receive the packet other than $\text{D}?$

  1. $\text{A}$
  2. $\text{B}$
  3. $\text{C}$
  4. $\text{E}$

An upper-layer packet is split into $10$ frames, each of which has an $80$ percent chance of arriving undamaged. If no error control is done by the data link protocol, how many times must the message be sent on average to get the entire thing through?

  1. $7.4$
  2. $9.3$
  3. $6.7$
  4. $2.4$

Suppose a router has built up the routing table shown below. The router can deliver packets directly over interfaces $0$ and $1,$ or it can forward packets to routers $\mathrm{R} 2, \mathrm{R} 3$, or $\mathrm{R} 4$.
$$
\begin{array}{l|l|l}
\hline \text{SubnetNumber} & \text{SubnetMask} & \text{NextHop} \\
\hline 128.96 .39 .0 & 255.255 .255 .128 & \text{Interface 0} \\
128.96 .39 .128 & 255.255 .255 .128 & \text{Interface 1} \\
128.96 .40 .0 & 255.255 .255 .128 & \text{R2} \\
192.4 .153 .0 & 255.255 .255 .192 & \text{R3} \\
\langle \text{default} \rangle & & \text{R4} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$
Which the following statements is/are true:

  1. For a packet addressed to the destination $128.96.39.10,$ router uses $\text{R4}$ as the next hop.
  2. For a packet addressed to the destination $128.96.40.12,$ router uses $\mathrm{R} 2$ as the next hop.
  3. For a packet addressed to the destination $192.4.153.17,$ router uses $\text{R3}$ as the next hop.
  4. For a packet addressed to the destination $192.4.153.90,$ router uses $\mathrm{R} 4$ as the next hop.

The routing table below uses the longest prefix match in its routing decisions.
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline \text{Network Address/Length} & \text{Next Hop} \\
\hline \hline 196.94 .8 .0 / 21 & \text{S} \\
\hline 196.94 .16 .0 / 24 & \text{T} \\
\hline 196.94 .0 .0 / 16 & \text{U} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
What are the next hops for each of the following two destination addresses?

$\begin{array}{lcc} & \text{Next Hop to} & \text{Next Hop to} \\  & \underline{196.94.10.7} & \underline{196.94.34.9} \\ \text{(A)} & \text{S} & \text{T} \\  \text{(B)} & \text{S} & \text{U} \\  \text{(C)} & \text{T} & \text{T} \\  \text{(D)} & \text{T} & \text{U}  \end{array}$
The valid host range that has the $\textsf{IP}$ address $172.29.217.11/22$ a part of, is $172.29.\text{X.Y}$ to $172.29.\text{Z.P}.$ Then $\mathrm{X}+\mathrm{Y}+\mathrm{Z}+\mathrm{P}$ is ?

A router has the following $\textsf{CIDR}$ entries in its forwarding table:
$$
\begin{array}{|l|l|}
\hline \text{Address/mask} & \text{Next hop}\\
\hline 135.46 .56 .0 / 22 & \text{Interface A} \\
135.46 .60 .0/22 & \text{Interface B} \\
135.46 .40 .0 / 23 & \text{Interface C}  \\
\text{Default} & \text{Interface D} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
If a packet with the $\textsf{IP address} \;135.46 .63 .10$ arrives, where does the router forward it?

  1. $\text{A}$
  2. $\text{B}$
  3. $\text{C}$
  4. $\text{D}$

In a $\textsf{CSMA/CD}$ network with a data rate of $10 \mathrm{~Mbps}$, the maximum distance between any station pair is found to be $2500 \mathrm{~m}$ for the correct operation of the collision detection process. What should be the maximum distance if we increase the date rate to $100 \mathrm{~Mbps}?$

  1. $25 \mathrm{~m}$
  2. $2500 \mathrm{~m}$
  3. $250 \mathrm{~m}$
  4. $25 \mathrm{~km}$

We have used even parity to construct a hamming code of $7$ bits using $4$ data bits and $3$ parity bits. Receiver receives $1011011$ codeword. If the channel can have utmost one bit of error then which of the following is true ?

  1. Recieved codeword is correct
  2. Recieved codeword is incorrect, and third bit from left end has been flipped during transmission
  3. Recieved codeword is incorrect, and third bit from right end has been flipped during transmission
  4. Recieved codeword is incorrect, and first bit from left end has been flipped during transmission

A sliding window protocol needs a sufficiently large window to avoid $\text{“stop and wait".}$  We have decided that a window size of $200$ is needed for a given communication link. Determine the (minimum) number of bits in sequence numbers with go-back-$n$ and selective repeat protocol.

  1. $8$ for Go Back $\text{N}$ Protocol
  2. $8$ for Selective Repeat Protocol
  3. $9$ for Go Back $\text{N}$ Protocol
  4. $9$ for Selective Repeat Protocol

Consider a sliding–window transfer mechanism where both the sender and receiver use a window of size $3$. The retransmission timeout (RTO) is $2 \times \mathrm{RTT}$. Packets numbered $1$ through $6$ are to be sent.
Packets $3$ and $6$ are lost during their first transmission.

Each correctly received packet generates cumulative ACK.
Assume fast retransmission is implemented such that retransmission takes place either upon receipt of the first duplicate ACK or upon timeout.

Determine how many $\mathrm{RTTs}$ from the start elapse before packet $6$ is transmitted again.

  1. $3$
  2. $5$
  3. $6$
  4. $8$

Let $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ be two stations attempting to transmit on an Ethernet. $\text{A's}$ frames will be numbered $\text{A1, A2},$ and so on, and $\text{B's}$ similarly.
Suppose $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ simultaneously attempt to send frame $1.$ Consider the following events.

  • $\text{A1}$ collides with $\text{B1, A}$ wins backoff race immediately after the first collision of $\text{A1}.$
  • $\text{A2}$ collides with $\text{B1, A}$ wins backoff race immediately after the first collision of $\text{A2}.$
  • $\text{A3}$ collides with $\text{B1}.$

What is the probability that $\text{A}$ wins this third backoff race immediately after the first collision of $\text{A3}?$

  1. $5 / 8$
  2. $13 / 16$
  3. $6 / 16$
  4. $3 / 4$
